candidates.quote: The unexamined life is not worth living.
candidates.author: Plato
candidates.locator: 38a, in the sentence beginning ‘and if I say again’; the capital and the full stop mark a cut at a complete clause. Verified in Jowett, Gutenberg 1656
candidates.speaker: Socrates
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest counsel in the language about paying attention to your own life, and six in the morning is when a person is best placed to take it.

candidates.quote: So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
candidates.author: Boethius
candidates.locator: Book II, Prose IV. Verified verbatim in the H. R. James text, Gutenberg 14328
candidates.speaker: Philosophy
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel from a consoler who needed consoling himself: the mood you wake in is not the day, and equanimity is something you bring rather than find.

candidates.quote: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
candidates.author: Francis Bacon
candidates.work: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
candidates.locator: Of Studies, the 1625 edition. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 575
candidates.whyThisMonth: Three habits named in one breath, and a reader at six in the morning has just chosen the first of them.

candidates.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
candidates.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
candidates.locator: the passage on envy and imitation, 1841 first edition. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 16643, where a bracketed note number follows the colon
candidates.whyThisMonth: The counsel Emerson is remembered for, and the one hardest to take at the hour when the day has not yet agreed with you.

candidates.quote: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
candidates.author: John Stuart Mill
candidates.locator: chapter II, Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion. Verified verbatim, Gutenberg 34901
candidates.whyThisMonth: Advice for anyone about to be certain about something before breakfast, which is most of us.

candidates.quote: I do not care what case you put; let them be sea-captains, if you will.
candidates.author: Margaret Fuller
candidates.locator: the passage on what offices women may fill. Verified verbatim in the Arthur B. Fuller edition of 1855, Gutenberg 8642; first published 1845
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence the book is remembered by: counsel to stop asking what a person is permitted to be and start asking what they can do.

candidates.quote: In order to be happy, one must have freed oneself of prejudices, one must be virtuous, healthy, have tastes and passions, and be susceptible to illusions; for we owe most of our pleasures to illusions, and unhappy is the one who has lost them.
candidates.author: Émilie du Châtelet
candidates.locator: the statement of the conditions of happiness; Selected Philosophical and Scientific Writings, Chicago, 2009, pp. 345 to 366. HEDGE: the page was not opened, the wording follows the Bour and Zinsser translation as scholars quote it
candidates.translator: Isabelle Bour and Judith P. Zinsser, 2009
candidates.whyThisMonth: A working list of what a happy life actually requires, written by a woman for herself and not for print, which is why it is honest.

candidates.quote: Sweet words are like hony, a little may refresh, but too much gluts the stomach.
candidates.author: Anne Bradstreet
candidates.locator: meditation IX. Verified in The Works of Anne Bradstreet in Prose and Verse, ed. J. H. Ellis, 1867, p. 50, whose spelling hony and whose comma these are; modern editions print honey and a semicolon
candidates.whyThisMonth: A mother's maxim, written out by hand for her son to keep, and a caution against the kind of sweetness a morning offers itself.

candidates.quote: One day as I was sitting alone in my study surrounded by books on all kinds of subjects.
candidates.author: Christine de Pizan
candidates.work: The Book of the City of Ladies
candidates.locator: Part I, ch. 1, the opening sentence, cut at a complete clause; Persea Books, 1982, p. 3. HEDGE: only as far as ‘surrounded by books’ was confirmed, the rest follows Richards as commonly quoted
candidates.whyThisMonth: Europe's first professional woman of letters opens her book exactly where the reader is sitting: alone, early, among books.

candidates.quote: Your silence will not protect you.
candidates.author: Audre Lorde
candidates.locator: The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action; Crossing Press, 1984, p. 41. Delivered as a panel paper in 1977 and printed in 1978 before the book, which a verifier should weigh against the rule on oratory
candidates.whyThisMonth: Five words of counsel about the thing you have been putting off saying, which at six in the morning is usually still unsaid.

candidates.quote: The cause of freedom is not the cause of a race or a sect, a party or a class,—it is the cause of human kind, the very birthright of humanity.
candidates.author: Anna Julia Cooper
candidates.locator: Woman versus the Indian, pp. 120 to 121, Aldine Printing House, 1892. Verified verbatim; the comma and dash are the 1892 setting
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel against the small circle: whatever you are working for today is worth more if it is not only for your own.

candidates.quote: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
candidates.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
candidates.locator: proposition 7, the closing line. Verified verbatim in the Ogden text, Gutenberg 5740
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous last line in modern philosophy, and permission for a morning that does not yet have words for itself.

candidates.quote: Do nothing which is of no use.
candidates.author: Miyamoto Musashi
candidates.locator: the Ground Book, the last of the nine rules for learning the Way; Overlook Press, 1974. HEDGE: the Harris wording was corroborated only from secondary sources, not from the printed page
candidates.whyThisMonth: The ninth and shortest of the rules a swordsman left behind, and the one that survives translation into an ordinary Tuesday.

candidates.quote: Good things, when short, are twice as good.
candidates.author: Baltasar Gracián
candidates.locator: maxim cv, Don’t be a Bore; Macmillan, first edition 1892, pp. 60 to 61. Verified verbatim in the Jacobs text
candidates.whyThisMonth: A maxim about maxims from the book that taught Europe to write them, and short enough that a reader carries it all day.

candidates.quote: Riches are for the sake of making life comfortable, not life for the sake of amassing riches.
candidates.author: Saadi
candidates.locator: chapter VIII, On the Duties of Society, Maxim I; Trübner, second edition, 1880, p. 205. Verified verbatim in the Eastwick text
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first maxim in Saadi's chapter of rules for living, and it puts the day's work back in its place before the work starts.

candidates.quote: If all Men are born Free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?
candidates.author: Mary Astell
candidates.locator: the Preface added in the third edition of 1706. Verified verbatim in Some Reflections upon Marriage, with Additions, 1730, p. 150, whose capitals these are
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel in the form of a question that took two hundred years to answer, in the manner of the Wollstonecraft rebuke already held for this month.
